title: XCON and commercial expert systems
text:
CHAPTER 12. EXPERT SYSTEMS
SECTION 12.2. XCON AND COMMERCIAL EXPERT SYSTEMS

DENDRAL and MYCIN (Section 12.1) showed that expert-level knowledge could be captured in programs. XCON showed that this could make money. Section 11.2 told the business story of the 1980s boom and bust; this section looks inside the technology: the forward-chaining production systems that XCON used, the Rete algorithm that made them fast, the shells and tools that turned expert systems into a product category, and the rule engines that still run in industry today. For a mechatronics engineer this is close to home: rule-based logic is how much industrial control, diagnostics and configuration software is still written.

1. The configuration problem

In the late 1970s Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) sold VAX minicomputers that customers ordered as combinations of many components: processors, memory boards, disk and tape drives, controllers, cabinets, power supplies, cables. A valid configuration had to satisfy many constraints: which boards fit in which slots of a backplane, bus loads and lengths, power budgets, cable lengths between cabinets, and the physical layout on the floor. Getting it wrong meant missing parts at the customer site, delays and dissatisfied customers, sometimes leading to disputes. Human technical editors checked orders, but it was slow and error-prone.

2. R1/XCON

John McDermott of Carnegie Mellon University began R1 in 1978 (the name reportedly came from a joke, "Four years ago I couldn't even say 'knowledge engineer,' and now I are one"; the system was renamed XCON, "eXpert CONfigurer," inside DEC). It was written in OPS5 and went into use in 1980 at DEC's plant in Salem, New Hampshire. McDermott described it in "R1: An Expert in the Computer Systems Domain" (1980).

Results commonly cited: by 1986 XCON had processed about 80,000 orders with 95 to 98 percent accuracy, and it was estimated to have saved DEC about 40 million dollars over six years (other sources give different figures). It eventually had about 2,500 rules in one count, with later versions growing larger, and DEC built related systems: XSEL (helping salespeople select components) and others in a family sometimes called "XCON and beyond."

The key technical point: XCON did not search. McDermott found that experts configured systems by a fixed sequence of subtasks (check the order for completeness, place components in the CPU cabinet, place components in the unibus cabinets, lay out the floor plan, assign cables), and that within each subtask, local knowledge was enough to make each decision correctly without backtracking. This "match" method, recognizing which action is right from the current situation, was efficient because the knowledge was sufficient. The difficulty was in the volume and variety of knowledge, not in combinatorial search.

3. Production systems and OPS5

OPS5 (Official Production System, version 5) was developed by Charles Forgy at Carnegie Mellon in the late 1970s, building on Allen Newell's group's research on production systems as models of human cognition. An OPS5 program has:

  - working memory: a set of working memory elements (WMEs), each a record of attribute-value pairs, like (component ^type disk ^model RA81 ^placed no);
  - production memory: rules of the form (p name condition-elements --> actions);
  - an inference engine running the recognize-act cycle.

A rule in OPS5 style:

    (p place-disk-in-cabinet
       (context ^task place-disks)
       (component ^type disk ^model <m> ^placed no)
       (cabinet ^id <c> ^free-slots { <n> > 0 })
    -->
       (modify 2 ^placed yes ^cabinet <c>)
       (modify 3 ^free-slots (compute <n> - 1)))

Variables in angle brackets bind consistently across conditions; "modify 2" refers to the second condition's matched element.

The recognize-act cycle (forward chaining):

    loop:
        match:    find all instantiations (rule + matching WMEs) whose
                  conditions are satisfied -> the conflict set
        resolve:  choose one instantiation by a conflict resolution strategy
        act:      execute its actions (make, modify, remove WMEs)
        until no rule matches or a halt action

This is data-driven, unlike MYCIN's goal-driven backward chaining. Forward chaining suits tasks like configuration, monitoring and control, where facts arrive and the system should react; backward chaining suits diagnosis, where there is a specific question to answer.

Conflict resolution. When several rules match, the engine must choose. OPS5 provided strategies called LEX and MEA. They combine:

  - refractoriness: an instantiation fires only once (prevents infinite loops on the same data);
  - recency: prefer instantiations using the most recently created or modified WMEs (keeps the system focused on the current line of work);
  - specificity: prefer rules with more conditions (more specific rules handle exceptions before general ones).

MEA (named after means-ends analysis) gives priority to recency of the first condition element, typically a "context" or goal element, which is how XCON structured its sequence of subtasks: rules that switch the context element move control from one subtask to the next. Many later engines also support explicit priorities (salience).

4. The Rete algorithm

The naive match step compares every rule against every combination of WMEs on every cycle. With R rules, W working memory elements and conditions of up to C elements, this costs roughly R * W^C per cycle, far too slow for thousands of rules and elements.

Charles Forgy's Rete algorithm (first described in a 1974 working paper, developed in his 1979 PhD thesis and published in a 1982 paper; "rete" is Latin for "net") exploits two observations:

  - Temporal redundancy: each cycle changes only a few WMEs, so most match results from the previous cycle are still valid. Store them and update incrementally.
  - Structural similarity: many rules share conditions. Share the tests.

Rete compiles all rules into a network:

  - Alpha network: tests on single WMEs (for example ^type disk). Each distinct test becomes one node shared by all rules using it. Each alpha memory stores the WMEs passing its tests.
  - Beta network: join nodes combine partial matches (tokens) from earlier conditions with WMEs from alpha memories, checking variable consistency (the same <c> in two conditions). Beta memories store the partial matches.
  - Terminal nodes: a token reaching the end of a rule's chain is a complete instantiation, added to the conflict set.

When a WME is added, it flows through the alpha tests; where it passes, it is joined with stored partial matches, possibly producing new ones. When a WME is removed, the matches containing it are removed. The cost per cycle depends on the number of changes and the affected partial matches, not on the total size of memory, so programs with thousands of rules became practical. The trade-off is memory: Rete stores many partial matches, and badly ordered conditions can create huge numbers of them. Later variants (TREAT, LEAPS, Rete II and others) trade memory for computation in different ways. Rete is still the basis of most production rule engines.

A tiny illustration. Rules R1: (A ^x <v>) (B ^x <v>) --> ... and R2: (A ^x <v>) (C ^x <v>) --> .... Both start with the test "class A," which becomes one shared alpha node. Adding (A ^x 5) passes that node and is joined once with stored B elements with x = 5 and C elements with x = 5. Nothing else in memory is re-examined.

5. Shells and tools

With the separation of knowledge base and inference engine pioneered by EMYCIN (Section 12.1), expert system "shells" became a product category in the 1980s. With a shell it was possible to enter some rules and have a prototype running in days rather than the months that conventional software projects took, which was a major selling point. Examples:

  - KEE (IntelliCorp) and ART (Inference Corporation): large, Lisp-based environments combining rules, frames (structured objects with slots and inheritance), and graphical interfaces, typically running on Lisp machines.
  - CLIPS ("C Language Integrated Production System"): developed from 1985 at NASA's Johnson Space Center, written in C for portability and speed on ordinary computers, with syntax inspired by OPS5. It was widely distributed and is still maintained as free software.
  - Smaller shells for personal computers, many using simple backward chaining.

A CLIPS rule (CLIPS is still easy to run today):

    (defrule overheat-alarm
       (sensor (id ?s) (type temperature) (value ?t&:(> ?t 90)))
       (not (alarm (sensor ?s)))
       =>
       (assert (alarm (sensor ?s) (level high)))
       (printout t "Overheat on sensor " ?s crlf))

Frames. Many commercial systems combined rules with frames, an idea proposed by Minsky in 1974: objects with named slots, default values and inheritance, such as a frame "Pump" with slots for flow rate, pressure and motor, and subframes "CentrifugalPump" inheriting the defaults. Frames are the ancestor of object-oriented knowledge representation and of the classes and ontologies used later in the semantic web.

6. Where commercial expert systems were used

Successful 1980s and early 1990s applications were narrow, high-value tasks where knowledge was stable and could be written down:

  - Configuration: XCON at DEC, and similar configurators for telephone switches and other complex products.
  - Diagnosis and troubleshooting: locomotive repair advisors, telephone line testing, equipment fault diagnosis.
  - Financial services: credit authorization, insurance underwriting, fraud screening.
  - Process monitoring and control: real-time expert systems (for example the G2 system from Gensym) monitored chemical plants and other processes, alarming and advising operators.
  - Scheduling and planning: such as the DART logistics tool (Section 11.2).
  - Law and regulation: a widely cited 1986 paper, "The British Nationality Act as a Logic Program," showed legislation encoded as Prolog rules.

Many systems gave real value, but the large market predicted in the early 1980s did not materialize, for the reasons covered in Sections 11.2 and 12.3.

7. What survives: rule engines and decision logic

Rule-based technology did not die; it lost the "AI" label. Modern descendants include:

  - Business rules engines such as Drools (open source, Java, developed under JBoss and Red Hat; its engine was historically based on an enhanced Rete), IBM Operational Decision Manager and others, used in banks, insurers and governments for eligibility, pricing and compliance rules. These separate frequently changing business logic from application code so that analysts can edit rules.
  - Product configurators (CPQ, "configure, price, quote" software) for complex products, the direct descendants of XCON, now often built on constraint solvers.
  - Industrial automation: alarm management, interlocks and diagnostic rules in PLC and SCADA systems; PLC ladder logic and IEC 61131-3 programs are, in a sense, forward-chaining rule systems evaluated cyclically.
  - Clinical decision support: drug interaction alerts and guideline reminders in hospital systems.
  - Hybrid systems in 2026: large language models are frequently paired with explicit rules, constraint checks or "guardrails" written as rules, because rules are predictable and auditable.

Connection to PLCs. A PLC scan cycle (read inputs, evaluate the logic, write outputs, repeat) resembles a production system with all rules evaluated every cycle and no conflict resolution: every rung whose conditions are true sets its outputs. An expert system adds a working memory of symbolic facts, variable binding across conditions, and explicit choice among competing rules. Understanding both helps in designing supervisory logic above the real-time control layer.

8. Summary

  - XCON (R1), by John McDermott at CMU from 1978 and used at DEC from 1980, configured VAX orders; it reportedly processed about 80,000 orders by 1986 with 95-98 percent accuracy and saved DEC an estimated 40 million dollars over six years.
  - XCON used knowledge to avoid search, working through an ordered sequence of subtasks.
  - OPS5 production systems run a recognize-act cycle of match, conflict resolution (refractoriness, recency, specificity; LEX and MEA) and act; this is forward chaining.
  - Forgy's Rete algorithm (1974, 1979 thesis, 1982 paper) makes matching incremental and shares tests across rules, making large rule bases practical.
  - Shells (KEE, ART, CLIPS from NASA in 1985) separated engines from knowledge; frames added structured objects.
  - Rule technology survives in business rules engines (Drools), configurators, industrial alarm and diagnostic logic, and guardrails around modern AI.
